c.tagline: Gleaming white marble monuments amid the Karakum Desert.

taxi.color: mostly white or unmarked private cars
taxi.fareNote: Meters are rare; agree on the fare, ideally in writing, before the ride, especially from the airport.

emergency.note: Fire is 01. English-speaking response capacity is limited; hotel staff or a tour guide are often the fastest route to help.

avoid.reason: Heavily controlled — avoid photographing government/military buildings; carry ID at all times

hood_desc: Ashgabat's marble-clad hotel and government strip along Archabil Highway, packed with fountains, parks and modern towers; suits travelers who want polish and comfort but don't mind taxiing everywhere.
The most walkable, lived-in part of town around Turkmenbashy Avenue and the Gulistan (Russian) Bazaar, near the train station; suits budget travelers wanting easier access to everyday local life.
A quieter southern district built around the 2017 Asian Games venues; a calm, less showy base good for those attending events or wanting distance from the marble showpiece core.

water.note: Avoid tap water; use bottled or filtered water.

transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash in manat directly to the driver or conductor; there is no rechargeable transit card for visitors. Fares are just a few cents, but exact change is appreciated. Shared minivan (marshrutka) routes are also common.
transit.hours: Buses and trolleybuses run roughly 6:00-23:00; there is no dedicated night bus network, so taxis are the only late-night option.
transit.note: Routes aren't published in English and drivers navigate by landmark rather than street name; having your destination written in Russian or Turkmen helps a lot.

train: Ashgabat Railway Station (domestic trains to Turkmenabat, Mary, Dashoguz and Turkmenbashy)
bus: Intercity buses and marshrutkas from Ashgabat's main bus station to regional cities

transit.m: Public city bus into center (~30-40 min)

tip.r: Not a deeply rooted custom; rounding up or leaving roughly 5-10% at restaurants used by tourists is appreciated but not expected elsewhere.

food.name: Dograma
food.desc: Chorek bread crumbled by hand into a bowl with boiled mutton, raw onion and hot broth poured over. The national dish, eaten with a spoon and no fork.

places.name: Ayak-Ui
places.note: Authentic Turkmen restaurant that keeps dograma, palaw and ichlekli on the permanent menu.

places.name: Kopetdag cafe
places.note: Open kitchen and yurt-style booths; a favourite for traditional cooking done in view.

places.name: Russian Bazaar canteens
places.note: Market cook shops serve dograma in the morning for a fraction of restaurant prices.

food.name: Palaw
food.desc: Turkmen pilaf: rice cooked down in mutton fat with carrot, onion and whole garlic in a wide kazan, served in a mound to share.

places.name: Kopetdag cafe
places.note: Chefs cook the palaw in the open kitchen; ask when the next kazan is due out.

places.name: Ayak-Ui
places.note: Traditional decor and a straightforward Turkmen palaw, best ordered at lunch.

places.name: Soltan Restaurant
places.note: Grand oriental dining room mixing Turkmen, Central Asian and Georgian cooking.

food.name: Ichlekli
food.desc: A large flat pie of thin dough filled with chopped mutton, onion and pumpkin, traditionally baked buried in hot sand and ash so the crust smokes.

places.name: Ayak-Ui
places.note: One of the reliable places in the capital to find ichlekli made the traditional way.

places.name: Altyn Asyr Bazaar food row
places.note: The huge weekend bazaar has bakers turning out meat pies straight from the ovens.

places.name: Kopetdag cafe
places.note: Serves the baked meat pies alongside its plov; good for a shared table.

food.name: Chorek
food.desc: Round tandyr-baked bread with a blistered crust, slapped onto the clay oven wall. Never place it upside down - Turkmens treat bread as close to sacred.

places.name: Russian Bazaar tandyr bakeries
places.note: Bread comes out of the clay ovens all morning; buy it while it still burns your hands.

places.name: Teke Bazaar
places.note: Central market bread row with several tandyr bakers working side by side.

places.name: Altyn Asyr Bazaar
places.note: Bread stacked in towers at the country's biggest market, alongside carpets and camels.

food.name: Manty
food.desc: Big steamed dumplings pleated around minced lamb, onion and pumpkin, eaten with sour cream or a splash of vinegar.

places.name: Ayak-Ui
places.note: Steamed to order in the Turkmen style, generously sized and cheap.

places.name: Soltan Restaurant
places.note: Polished setting for manty and other Central Asian standards; popular for dinner.

places.name: Russian Bazaar canteens
places.note: Market kitchens sell manty by the piece from stacked steamer baskets.

food.name: Gutap
food.desc: Half-moon turnovers fried until blistered and filled with minced meat, pumpkin or a handful of spring greens - the Turkmen street snack of choice.

places.name: Russian Bazaar food stalls
places.note: Fried to order at the market snack counters; the greens version appears in spring.

places.name: Teke Bazaar
places.note: Handy central market stop for gutap and samsa between sightseeing stops.

places.name: Kopetdag cafe
places.note: Serves gutap as a starter before the plov and grilled meat.

food.name: Chal
food.desc: Fermented camel's milk - fizzy, sharp and faintly salty, drunk cold in summer and credited by Turkmens with curing almost anything.

places.name: Altyn Asyr Bazaar dairy row
places.note: The most likely place to find genuine chal, sold from churns by desert herders.

places.name: Russian Bazaar dairy sellers
places.note: Bottled chal and sour milk drinks kept on ice through the summer months.

places.name: Ayak-Ui
places.note: Traditional restaurant that usually has chal on the drinks list beside the tea.

food.name: Gok chai
food.desc: Green tea poured from a china pot into small bowls and drunk scalding hot even at 40 degrees - the constant of every Turkmen table and negotiation.

places.name: Kopetdag cafe
places.note: Tea served in the yurt booths, the traditional way to end a meal here.

places.name: Soltan Restaurant
places.note: Pots of green tea with sweets and dried fruit after dinner.

places.name: Teke Bazaar tea stalls
places.note: Traders' tea corners in the market - the cheapest and most sociable pour in town.

landmarks: Arch of Neutrality
This tripod-legged monument topped by a golden statue of the former president offers panoramic views over Ashgabat from its elevated observation deck.
Independence Monument
This towering minaret-like spire crowned with a crescent moon and stars commemorates Turkmenistan's independence and anchors a grand surrounding park.
Wedding Palace (Bagt Koshgi)
This surreal star-shaped skyscraper wrapped in a giant golden globe is where Ashgabat couples marry, making it one of the world's most bizarre wedding venues.
National Museum of Turkmenistan
This grand marble museum houses priceless artifacts from ancient Silk Road cities like Nisa and Merv, tracing millennia of Turkmen history.
Monument to the Constitution
One of the tallest structures in the city, this star-topped tower symbolizes Turkmenistan's constitutional order amid the capital's forest of white marble monuments.
Nisa
The hilltop ruins of Old Nisa, one of the earliest Parthian cities, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2007 where excavators uncovered carved ivory rhytons.
Türkmenbaşy Ruhy Mosque (Kipchak Mosque)
One of Central Asia's largest mosques, this vast marble-domed complex near the late president's mausoleum can hold tens of thousands of worshippers at once.
Ertugrul Gazi Mosque
Modeled on Istanbul's Blue Mosque, this striking Ottoman-style mosque with its slender minarets and cascading domes stands out even amid Ashgabat's marble skyline.
Alem Cultural and Entertainment Center
This glass-domed complex houses the world's largest enclosed Ferris wheel, letting visitors ride high above Ashgabat regardless of the desert heat outside.
Independence Park
This sprawling landscaped park surrounding the Independence Monument features fountains, statues, and manicured gardens celebrating Turkmen national heritage.

train.note: There are currently no international passenger trains from Turkmenistan - the old Serakhs-Mashhad line to Iran has stayed suspended since the pandemic. Domestic sleepers run from Ashgabat to Turkmenabat, Dashoguz, Mary and Turkmenbashi, but tickets are bought in person at the station rather than online, and foreigners need a valid Turkmen visa/permit. HUMAN EDITOR: verify the railway.gov.tm domain is live and correct before publishing.

bus.note: There are no practical scheduled international coaches out of Ashgabat; Turkmenistan is tightly controlled and land borders are often closed to foreigners. Long-distance travel within the country is by domestic bus and shared taxi. Check current entry rules, as independent overland transit usually requires a pre-arranged tour or transit visa.

ferry.note: The only international boat is the Caspian ferry between Turkmenbashi and Baku (Azerbaijan). Turkmenbashi is about 560 km west of Ashgabat (reachable by domestic train or flight), and the ships are cargo/Ro-Ro vessels that also take passengers with no fixed timetable - be ready to wait, and arrange your onward visa in advance.

half.name: Gökdepe
half.blurb: Site of the 1880-81 siege, when Russian troops stormed the Turkmen fortress in January 1881, now marked by the Saparmyrat Hajji Mosque.

half.name: Anau
half.blurb: Ruins of the 15th-century Timurid Seyit Jemaleddin Mosque, largely toppled by the 1948 earthquake, beside ancient Anau.

full.name: Kow Ata Underground Lake
full.blurb: A cave in the Kopet Dag foothills where visitors descend to swim in a warm, sulphurous underground lake.

laundry.note: No self-service laundromats use your hotel laundry service

gyms.note: Confirmed operating mixed gym (separate Dynamics for Ladies branch at house 31). No published single-visit or day-pass price found; contact is by phone only.
Fitness club located inside Ashgabat Stadium. No published day/single-visit price found online; directory listing only confirms existence and location.
